title: Heterogeneous Slot Tiering and Probabilistic Headroom Optimizer for GPU Memory Budgeting
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Problem statement:
We have recurring operational pain from tail OOMs and large variances in tail latency across mixed workloads when continuous batching and KV cache usage interact. Existing soft-watermark approaches are brittle for multi-tenant skew: large KV footprints from long-chat sessions plus bursty activation patterns cause aggressive KV eviction or weight offloads and destabilize latency SLOs.

Goal:
Design and implement a GPU memory budgeting system that: (1) explicitly partitions memory into heterogeneous "slots" for weights (pinned), KV cache (shared slab with tiering), and ephemeral activations; (2) computes a probabilistic headroom buffer per GPU that adapts to tail-latency forecasts and tenant mix; (3) exposes a rebalancer that migrates KV slabs and throttles batching rules preemptively rather than reactively after pressure; (4) integrates with existing telemetry and rollout controls in the console.

High-level design summary:
- Heterogeneous slot tiering: divide GPU device memory into three logical tiers: WEIGHTS (static pinned region by model/variant), KV-SHARED (slab allocator subdivided into hot/cold lanes), and EPHEMERAL (activation pool with elastic corridor). Slots are enforced by allocator hints and a lightweight memory ledger.
- Probabilistic headroom estimator: use a quantile-based forecast (q=0.99, configurable) of short-term activation growth and KV retention to set a soft headroom margin that trades throughput for safety. Forecast uses recent per-route sequence length histogram, predicted burst probability, and tenant-level KV retention metrics.
- KV slab tiering: split KV-SHARED into HOT and COLD lanes. HOT lane holds high-reuse prefixes (LRU-windowed by token-frequency + recency score). COLD lane is amenable to probabilistic partial eviction (sampling-based) and compressible entries. A background cold-compressor reduces footprint under pressure.
- Preemptive rebalancer: when headroom estimator indicates >X% probability of crossing safety threshold within T seconds, the rebalancer can (a) reduce batching target sizes for affected routes, (b) migrate cold KV pages to remote/shrink encoding, (c) temporarily increase on-device weight offload threshold for low-priority tenants. All actions are ordered by cost model to minimize downstream tail latency impact.
- Safety policy and graceful degradation: define ordered fallback actions (throttle batching -> compress KV cold -> migrate cold pages -> tenant degrade) with per-tenant QoS tags. Add a fast OOM-avoid path that drains ephemeral activations to a preallocated spill buffer rather than abruptly killing requests.

Implementation plan (milestones):
1) Simulation harness update (week 1-2): extend the memory simulator to model HOT/COLD KV lanes, probabilistic bursts, and rebalancer actions. Run simulations across tenants mixes (chatty long-session, short completion, high-throughput small-seq).
2) Allocator primitives (week 2-4): add allocator hints and a lightweight ledger to the runtime; implement slot enforcement hooks; unit tests.
3) Headroom estimator (week 3-5): implement quantile-forecasting service integrated with per-GPU telemetry; expose estimator REST endpoint for the rebalancer.
4) KV slab manager (week 4-6): HOT/COLD lanes, sampling-based cold eviction, cold-compressor, and APIs to mark pages for migration/compression.
5) Rebalancer + policy engine (week 5-7): decision logic implementing cost model, ordered actions, and safe cooldown windows.
6) Canary rollout and observability (week 7-9): integrate console dashboard with headroom signal, action logs, KPIs (eviction rate, tail latency, OOMs, throughput, cost-per-token). Run canary on a small dedicated capacity pool.

Telemetry and KPIs:
- OOM incidents per 10k reqs (target: reduce by >= 90% on canary workloads)
- 99th percentile latency delta vs baseline (target: <+15ms)
- KV cold-eviction rate and compressor throughput
- Successful preemptive rebalancer interventions vs reactive actions
- Per-token GPU cost change (should be neutral or improved over time)

Testing and validation:
- Integration tests with multi-tenant simulated traffic (replay using production anonymized histograms).
- Chaos tests: sudden long-session surge, KV-retention spike, synthetic activation storm. Ensure rebalancer prevents OOMs and keeps tail latency within SLO.
- Fallback validation: confirm spill buffer semantics and correctness of temporary batching throttles.

Rollout plan:
- Feature gated by config boolean and per-cluster control.
- Start with internal dedicated pool (non-customer traffic), then low-risk customers on Dedicated for 2 weeks, then opt-in Private customers. Monitor KPIs and alarms.

Risk and trade-offs:
- Complexity: introduces a more complex allocator + policy engine; mitigated by careful feature gates and observability.
- Throughput regression risk when headroom margin increases; mitigated by cost-model ordering and conservative default thresholds.
- Migration and compression CPU overhead; background work must be rate-limited and capped per-GPU.

Open decisions / follow-ups needed:
- Default quantile level and prediction window (proposal: q=0.99, window=60s). Requires experimentation.
- Spill buffer sizing policy: fixed per-GPU vs dynamic.
- Tenant QoS tags taxonomy and priority mapping for policy engine.
